sentences.text: Yui and her mother took the train to Otsu on a Sunday afternoon.
It was not a long ride from Kyoto — only fifteen minutes — but Yui had brought her old shiba dog Momo with her, and Momo did not like the train.
He was fifteen years old, which was very old for a shiba, and he did not like anything new anymore, and he had spent the whole ride pressed against Yui's leg making small worried sounds.
When they got off at Otsu station, Yui knelt down and put her face against his neck for a moment before they walked to Ojiisan's house.
Ojiisan lived alone in the same small wooden house he had lived in for forty years, five streets back from the shore of Lake Biwa.

Yui was ten and she had been to Ojiisan's house every summer for as long as she could remember, but this was the first time she had come without her mother — her mother was going back on the evening train, because there was a work thing.
Yui was staying for a whole week, alone.
Just her and Ojiisan.
And Momo.
Ojiisan was very glad to see Yui.
He had made cold barley tea and small round rice balls for her, and he had put out a soft folded blanket in the corner of the main room for Momo, because he had known Momo since Momo was a puppy.
After Yui's mother left, they sat at the low table together and ate the rice balls, and they did not talk very much.
Ojiisan was a quiet man.
That was one of the things Yui liked best about him.
She never had to think of what to say.
After they ate, Yui went out onto the wooden engawa porch that ran along the back of the house.
It faced the small garden — a bit of moss, some carefully placed stones, and a low wall around it all.
Beyond the wall, if you looked between the roofs of the other houses, you could just see a strip of grey water, which was the lake.
She sat down on the porch.
Momo followed her, slowly, and lay down next to her with a long slow sigh, and she put her hand on his back.
Ojiisan came out too, and sat on her other side.
They sat like that for a while, watching the garden.
Yui was thinking about Momo.
He had been slower this year than last, and thinner, and he slept most of the day now, and sometimes he woke up in the night and cried a little, softly.
Her mother had said Momo was very old, and that Yui should be ready for what would come.
Yui was ready.
She thought she was ready.
She was not sure.
"Ojiisan," she said.
"Yes." "When Baba died, were you very sad." Ojiisan was quiet for a long moment.
Baba was Ojiisan's wife, Yui's grandmother, and she had died before Yui was born.
He turned to look at her, then looked back out at the garden.
"Yes," he said.
"I was very sad." Yui nodded.
She had thought so.
"There is a story from around here," Ojiisan said, after a while.
"An old story.
About what happens when someone is very sad.
My grandmother told it to me when I was your age." "What is it," said Yui.
Ojiisan settled himself.
He was a good teller of stories, even though he did not tell many.
He waited until the light in the garden went a little more golden.
Then he began.
"When someone in Otsu is very sad — really sad, so sad they cannot eat or sleep or think — a grey cat comes.
She is not a normal cat.
She has been in Otsu for many hundreds of years.
She comes to the house of the sad person, and she sits on the wall of the garden, and she watches.
She does not come inside, unless she is invited.
If you notice her, and if you want her to stay, you leave a small dish of water on the porch.
Then she stays for three days.
She does not speak.
She does not do anything special.
She only sits with you."
"And then what," said Yui.
"Then, on the third day, she goes.
She does not come back.
Not for you.
Not ever.
She is only for one sadness.
And the story is that when she is with you, the sadness is a little easier.
Not gone.
Just easier.
As if there is someone else carrying part of it." Yui thought about this.
She was ten and she did not always believe things people told her, but she also did not disbelieve them right away, because she knew she did not know everything yet.
"Have you seen her," she said.
Ojiisan smiled a small sad smile.
"Once," he said.
"When Baba died.
She came the day after the funeral.
She sat on that wall right there." He pointed.
"For three days.
I put water out for her.
On the third evening, she was gone.
She did not eat the food I put out.
I only saw her drink from the water twice, and only a little.
But she stayed." Yui watched the wall.
Nothing was on it.
The garden was still.
"Do you think she was real," she said.
Ojiisan did not answer for a long time.
Then he said, "I think it does not matter whether she was real.
That is not the important part."
